dataset_differences: Only TACO and ARCTIC were analysed in this diagnostic; there is no OakInk2 result for these blocks.

Alignment (F3-diagB): Spearman(ΔC, Δz) is about 0.85 on TACO and 0.81 on ARCTIC at every horizon; ARCTIC intervals are wider (44 test takes against 186), e.g. h = 1: [0.766, 0.859] against [0.836, 0.866].

Rare exceptions (F3-diagB): low-ΔC / high-Δz transitions are 0.2 % on TACO and 0.5-0.7 % on ARCTIC (horizon mean 0.19 % / 0.60 %), i.e. about three times as frequent on ARCTIC. The opposite quadrant (high ΔC / low Δz) is 0.2-0.3 % on TACO and 0.0 % on ARCTIC.

What the exceptions are (post hoc): on TACO at h = 4, 47 % start from weak contact, 35 % carry a participation flip, 42 % a large teacher step, 21 % none of these; on ARCTIC the object articulates in 99 % / 100 % / 100 % of them (34-35 % of all test transitions do). The report calls the ARCTIC pattern 'consistent with the encoder reading the per-frame articulated geometry' and states that no ablation was run.

Persistence of z: ARCTIC z is more persistent (persistence R² at h = 1 / 4 / 8: 0.985 / 0.886 / 0.749) than TACO z (0.950 / 0.796 / 0.611). On both datasets z is less persistent than the dense map C (h = 8: C 0.90 TACO / 0.88 ARCTIC); the mean latent step is 2.2 / 2.1 / 1.9 times the mean contact step on TACO and 1.6 / 1.6 / 1.5 times on ARCTIC.
Window-averaged probe gain over persistence (rule input, F3-diagC): TACO 3.3 % / 11.3 % / 17.8 % (marginal / clear / clear); ARCTIC -2.6 % / 0.2 % / 6.9 % (no / no / marginal).

Rule outcome: Case A on TACO (borderline: h = 4 gain interval [9.95 %, 12.54 %], rescue 11.3 % [7.6, 15.2] on its 10 % line, and the h = 4 'clear' label needs the trajectory input) versus Case B on ARCTIC (a property of the window average). Rescue from the true z_0 (rule input): 11.3 % [7.6, 15.2] TACO versus 5.8 % [-2.6, 13.7] ARCTIC.

Post hoc by window position: at t = 0 the gain is clear on BOTH datasets (TACO 12 / 25 / 32 %, ARCTIC 23 / 27 / 28 %). For t = 1..7 TACO is 9 / 22 / 28 % while ARCTIC is indistinguishable from zero (-0.1 / 3.1 / 3.7 %). For t >= 8 TACO is 2 / 9 / 14 % while ARCTIC is -9 / -3 / 6 % (worse than persistence at h = 1).

Validation-to-test transfer: TACO validation gains largely hold on test (4.9 / 14.2 / 18.3 % against 3.3 / 11.3 / 17.8 %); ARCTIC validation gains (5.9 / 9.0 / 12.8 %) are gone on test at h = 1 and 4 and about halved at h = 8. 21 of the 44 ARCTIC test takes come from a subject (s10) absent from training; all ARCTIC validation takes are from training subjects. The report shows post hoc that the unseen subject costs gain only in the first eight frames and does not produce the Case B label.

Which predictor is best differs: on TACO the nonlinear probe with the trajectory is the best predictor at h = 4 and 8; on ARCTIC at h = 1 and 4 the nonlinear probe is not the best (the ridge gains 0.9 % / 2.2 % with intervals excluding zero, the probe -2.6 % / 0.2 %).

Decoded contact: the probe's latent gain shows up through the frozen decoder on TACO at h = 8 only (1.13 [1.07, 1.20] against 1.31 [1.25, 1.38]); on ARCTIC at no horizon (0.69 / 0.97 / 1.23 against 0.68 / 0.93 / 1.22).

Object-trajectory input (post hoc, paired): on TACO it adds +2.0 and +2.9 points at h = 4 and 8 (intervals exclude zero) and nothing at h = 1; on ARCTIC it costs -3.7 points [-6.4, -1.4] at h = 1 and adds +4.9 [-0.1, +9.3] at h = 8 (interval touches zero).
do_not_claim: Do not write that z's temporal behaviour is 'not the problem' or that the representation is cleared as a cause of the Stage-2 failure: only 'Case C as pre-registered (the steps of z do not follow the steps of the contact)' is rejected, and whether z's lower persistence than the dense map contributed was not tested.

Do not write 'the learned predictor beats persistence' for ARCTIC, or without the window-average qualifier: ARCTIC is -2.6 % / 0.2 % / 6.9 % (no / no / marginal), with intervals including zero at h = 1 and 4.

Do not write that ARCTIC z 'has no dynamics', 'is static' or that 'nothing beyond persistence is learnable': at the first frame of a window the ARCTIC gain is 23-28 %, and the ridge reference beats persistence at all three horizons.
Do not write 'the gain is smaller for later pairs on both datasets': on ARCTIC the probe is significantly worse than persistence at h = 1 for pairs starting at t >= 8 and indistinguishable at h = 4.

Do not present the window-position split (or the subject split, the linear references, the trajectory contrast, the composition of the exceptions) as pre-registered results or as rule inputs: they are post hoc ('interpretation, not verdicts').

Do not read the case letters as causes: 'Case A = Stage 2 failed because of open-loop prediction' and 'Case B = z has no learnable dynamics' are the pre-registered READINGS, which the decision table itself marks as not tested (no rollout, no horizon beyond 8) or as a window-average statement.

Do not write that a mixture of both causes was found, that neither hypothesis explains the Stage-2 failure, or that Q5 is answered: the report says 'not decided between A and B' and 'It is not a finding that both causes contribute'.

Do not write that a stateful / iterative / closed-loop z model will or does work better: no closed-loop rollout and no horizon beyond eight frames were measured; the report says 'its benefit is not established'. The stateful-z experiment is a motivated current hypothesis, not a result.

Do not call the probe result 'the dynamics of z' in an autonomous or causal sense: the probe is given the TRUE current latent plus the object-trajectory windows of frames t and t+h (including future object states), it is a single-step teacher-forced prediction, and on TACO about 60 % of its gain is linear in z_t alone.
Do not equate a latent gain with better contact: through the frozen decoder the gain appears only on TACO at h = 8, and on ARCTIC not at all.
Do not extrapolate the growth of the gain with the horizon (3 / 11 / 18 % on TACO) beyond h = 8.
Do not state the gains as seed-robust or as estimates of what is learnable: one seed, one probe family, early-stopped; the report calls them lower bounds on what is learnable.

Do not call the ARCTIC result a cross-subject artefact: on seen-subject test takes the labels are also no / no / marginal, and for t >= 8 the probe is as far below persistence on seen subjects (-8.2 %) as on the unseen one (-9.0 %).
Do not write that the articulated-geometry input explains the ARCTIC exceptions: the report says 'consistent with' and 'No ablation of the geometry input was run to confirm it'.
Do not pool or average the datasets (no 'Spearman 0.83 overall', no '0.4 % of transitions').

Do not present 0.2 % / 0.6 % as a per-horizon value (it is the mean over h = 1, 4, 8; ARCTIC is 0.7 % at h = 4) or the 7.5 % / 8.5 % independence expectation as a horizon mean (it is the h = 4 value).

Do not call the low-ΔC / high-Δz transitions 'errors' or 'noise' of the encoder: on TACO about a third to a half of them carry a structural (participation / teacher) step, i.e. z responds to the structure it was trained on at a small L2 footprint.
Do not write 'contact does not move over time' or 'z is smooth' without qualification: z moves 1.5-2.2 times as far as the dense map in random-pair units and is less persistent than C.

Do not describe the rule as externally pre-registered: say it was fixed in the code before the probes were trained, according to the report (no independent timestamp; one disclosed edit for the validation interval; the rule implementation was corrected once after review, cases unchanged).
Do not use 'disentangled', 'independent', 'proves', 'causes' or 'necessary' for anything in these blocks; z is 'structure-oriented' in the report's own wording.
